about: The Engineer in Society is a short Part IA course in the Cambridge Engineering Tripos on the economic, social, ethical and environmental contexts in which engineers work, delivered in 2025-26 as eight 50-minute talks by the module leader and guest speakers. It has no exam; it is assessed by a non-technical report of about 1000 words (plus or minus 10%) written over the Christmas vacation, with the title given in the final lecture and submission through Moodle. Under the 2026-27 Part IA coursework credit notice the report is marked 0-16, with 12 for satisfactory work and one mark lost per day late.
topics: What the module is and what the talks cover

notes.h: What The Engineer in Society is
notes.body:
The Engineer in Society is a short Part IA course in the Cambridge Engineering Tripos about the world engineers work in rather than the technical content of engineering. It has no exam questions and no fixed body of theory to revise. Instead it is assessed by a single non-technical report, so this pack is a guide to the module rather than a set of revision notes.

What it aims to do
- Introduce the economic, social, ethical and environmental settings in which engineers work, and how these are changing.
- Give a sense of the wider picture in which any engineering organisation operates, including questions of risk and security.
- Show why this context matters for engineering decisions, and highlight the non-technical skills (communication, judgement, working with people and organisations) that engineers need to succeed.

How it is taught
- In 2025-26 the course consisted of eight 50-minute presentations, given by the module leader and guest speakers from outside the department.
- Each talk is designed to supply material that will help with the report, so attendance and good notes matter more than in a typical lecture course.

What the talks covered in 2025-26
The published lecture list ran roughly as follows:
- What engineers actually do.
- How the world is changing for engineers.
- Manufactured environments, and whether they are a problem.
- Why it is so hard to bring about change for the better.
- Making a real-world impact with engineering skills.
- Getting hold of the resources needed to change things.
- Making really tough decisions.
- Engineering change to make the world better, which also covers how to pass the module.

The exact titles and speakers change from year to year, so check the current course page and Moodle for the 2026-27 list.

How it fits into Part IA
- The report is one of the Part IA coursework activities. Coursework counts towards the Part IA result alongside the four three-hour written papers, so the report is not optional.
- In 2025-26 there was no booklist for the module; online resources are provided through its Moodle site.

What to take from it
- Engineering decisions are rarely purely technical: cost, regulation, public acceptance, ethics, the environment and organisational politics all shape what actually gets built.
- Professional engineers are regularly asked to write clear, balanced responses to questions that do not have a single right answer. The report is practice for exactly that.

notes.h: The report: format, deadline and marking
notes.body:
Everything in this section comes from the department's course page and Part IA coursework credit notice. Details can change, so always check Moodle and the current course page before you start writing.

The task
- A non-technical report of about 1000 words. The allowed range is plus or minus 10%, so aim for roughly 900 to 1100 words.
- It is written over the Christmas vacation.
- The title and detailed instructions are released in the final lecture of the module, so you cannot start the actual report early. You can, however, collect material from every talk.
- The purpose is to give practice in writing a professional response to a non-technical question, something engineers do throughout their careers.

Submission
- Reports are submitted through the module's Moodle site.
- In 2025-26 the deadline was 16:00 on Friday 23 January 2026, early in Lent Term. Check the 2026-27 date on Moodle; do not assume it is the same.

Marking (Part IA coursework credit notice for 2026-27)
- The report is marked on a scale of 0 to 16.
- 12 marks are given for satisfactory work, and 12 is the qualifying mark for this activity.
- One mark is deducted for each day the report is late.
- For Part IA coursework in general, raw marks for each activity are capped at the qualifying level, so a satisfactory, on-time report secures the full credit for this item. A late or unsatisfactory report can lose marks that count towards your Part IA result.

How coursework fits into the overall result
- The credit notice states that the maximum raw coursework mark across all Part IA activities is 200 (the total of the qualifying marks), and the final coursework mark is the raw total minus 100, giving a maximum of 100.
- The four written papers are each marked out of 200, so with coursework the Part IA examination totals 900 marks.

Academic integrity
- The work you submit must be your own, following the department's guidance on plagiarism, cooperation and cheating.
- You must also follow the University and departmental guidelines on the use of artificial intelligence tools in submitted work. Read them before you begin; if in doubt, ask the module leader or your Director of Studies.

Practical checklist
- Note the deadline and plan to submit a few days early to avoid late penalties from technical problems.
- Keep within the word range and follow any formatting or referencing instructions given in the final lecture.
- Answer the question actually set, not a general essay on the module's themes.

notes.h: How to prepare and write a strong report
notes.body:
The report is short, so quality of thinking and clarity of writing count for more than volume. The advice below is general good practice for a non-technical professional report; the specific requirements in the title and instructions always take priority.

During the term
- Attend every talk. Each one is intended to give you material for the report, and guest speakers often give real examples you will not find elsewhere.
- Take notes that record the speaker's main argument, any concrete examples or case studies, and any sources or data they mention, so you can cite them later.
- After each talk, write two or three sentences on what it implies for how engineers should make decisions. These notes become your raw material.

Before writing
- Read the title and instructions carefully and underline the command words (for example "discuss", "evaluate", "recommend"). Decide exactly what question you are answering.
- Identify your audience. A non-technical report should be understandable to an intelligent reader without an engineering background, such as a manager, policymaker or member of the public.
- Plan a clear position or recommendation, and list the arguments for and against it.

Structure
- A short introduction that states the question and your main conclusion.
- A few focused sections, each making one point supported by evidence: an example from the talks, a real project, or a credible published source.
- Consider the economic, social, ethical and environmental angles the module emphasises, and acknowledge trade-offs and uncertainty rather than pretending there is one obvious answer.
- A conclusion that answers the question directly and, if asked, gives clear recommendations.

Style
- Use plain English, short paragraphs and informative headings. Avoid jargon; explain any technical term you cannot avoid.
- Be specific: a well-chosen example is worth more than general statements.
- Reference your sources consistently, as the instructions require.
- Keep within the 1000 words plus or minus 10% limit. Cutting a draft down usually improves it.

Before submitting
- Re-read against the title: does every paragraph help answer it?
- Check the word count, spelling and formatting.
- Make sure the work is entirely your own and consistent with the University and departmental guidance on AI tools.
- Submit on Moodle before the deadline, allowing time for upload problems.

Common pitfalls
- Writing a summary of the lectures instead of answering the question.
- Writing a technical report full of equations when a non-technical one was asked for.
- Ignoring the counter-arguments, or leaving the conclusion vague.
- Missing the deadline: every day late costs a mark.

questions.q: What mark is awarded for a satisfactory Engineer in Society report under the Part IA coursework credit notice?
questions.why: The report is marked on a 0–16 scale with 12 for satisfactory work, which is also the qualifying mark for the activity. 16 out of 16 confuses the top of the scale with the satisfactory mark; 8 out of 16 assumes a 50% pass threshold; 40 out of 100 borrows the 40% pass mark used in many UK degree schemes. None of these is how this report is credited.

questions.q: What happens if The Engineer in Society report is submitted two days late?
options: There is no penalty if it is satisfactory
questions.why: The credit notice deducts one mark per day late, so two days late costs two marks. It is not automatically marked zero, lateness is penalised even for satisfactory work, and the cap at the qualifying level applies to all reports, not as a late penalty.
